summary:
I developed Chronospectra, a public-facing, interactive web observatory built to explore multi-epoch, 102-band near-infrared sky surveys from NASA’s SPHEREx mission. Built with a Next.js and WorldWide Telescope (WWT) WebGL frontend paired with a FastAPI and Astropy/Zarr backend, the platform features a Dual-Axis Temporal-Spectral Matrix that lets users scrub simultaneously through six-month survey epochs and infrared wavelengths (0.75 to 5.0 µm), alongside an automated Cosmic Anomaly Radar that flags moving objects and flux shifts, on-the-fly Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) extraction, and a private observation logbook.

Chronospectra directly addresses the challenge of making SPHEREx’s massive, multi-dimensional datasets visually accessible and searchable for anyone. Instead of forcing users to manually sift through static FITS files or flat 1D image sliders, our tool transforms raw spectral cubes into fluid, interactive sky maps with URL coordinate deep-linking, multi-survey overlays (AllWISE/2MASS), and instant chemical/motion diagnostics.

This is important because SPHEREx maps over a billion celestial objects every six months, creating a treasure trove of moving brown dwarfs, asteroids, comets, and variable stars too vast for professional astronomers to analyze alone. Chronospectra empowers citizen scientists and researchers alike to rapidly uncover transient cosmic phenomena and chemical evolution across time.
details:
What it does and how it works

Chronospectra is a high-performance, public-facing web observatory designed to parse the massive near-infrared datasets generated by NASA’s SPHEREx mission. Instead of a standard 1D timeline slider, the platform features a Dual-Axis Temporal-Spectral Matrix. This allows users to simultaneously scrub through six-month time epochs (the X-axis) and 102 infrared light bands spanning 0.75 to 5.0 µm (the Y-axis).

Under the hood, a Python backend ingests raw Multi-Extension FITS (MEF) spectral cubes from NASA’s Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), converting them into web-friendly HiPS tiles for visual rendering and lightweight Zarr chunks for data extraction. The web interface utilizes the WorldWide Telescope (WWT) Web SDK to provide a smooth, 60 FPS 3D spherical sky map. As users navigate, an automated "Cosmic Anomaly Radar" runs a differential algorithm to flag significant flux shifts between epochs—such as moving brown dwarfs, comets, or variable stars—placing glowing pins on the map. Clicking any coordinate instantly queries the Zarr store to generate an interactive Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) chart, comparing epoch chemistry side-by-side. The tool also includes a "My Observations" logbook where users can create an account, save celestial objects, and prepare for future viewing sessions.

Benefits and Intended Impact

SPHEREx captures images of over a billion objects, creating a dataset too vast for professional astronomers to analyze alone. Chronospectra democratizes this data, translating complex astrophysics into an intuitive interface for citizen scientists and researchers. By automating anomaly detection and presenting chemical changes (like water or carbon dioxide ice absorption) visually, the project dramatically accelerates the discovery of transient cosmic phenomena. The intended impact is to crowdsource astronomical discovery, allowing anyone with a web browser to pitch in and spot the subtle shifts of new planets, asteroids, or erupting stars.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software

  • Frontend: Next.js (React), TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS.
  • Sky Rendering: WorldWide Telescope (WWT) Web SDK for programmatic camera control and high-performance WebGL spherical rendering.
  • Backend: FastAPI (Python) and a SQLite database for user authentication and logbook management.
  • Data Processing: Astropy, Astroquery, Healpy, and NumPy for querying NASA IRSA, handling HEALPix coordinates, and processing raw FITS files into HiPS and Zarr formats.
  • Hosting and Architecture: Vercel (frontend deployment), Render or Railway (backend hosting), and Cloudflare R2 for zero-egress cloud storage to serve heavy visual tiles globally without bandwidth bottlenecks.
"Science is not only a disciple of reason but, one of romance and passion." — Dr. Jocelyn Bell Burnell (Discoverer of pulsars)

How the project is creative

Chronospectra reimagines the standard astronomical archive as a cinematic, retro-futuristic telemetry dashboard. Rather than presenting static FITS images, the UI draws inspiration from professional audio mixing consoles, utilizing glowing tactical notches for its matrix controller and a custom dark-mode "obsidian and neon cyan" aesthetic. We integrated a plain-English "Cosmic Storyteller" script that parses complex spectral shifts and outputs simple narrative alerts (e.g., "Warning: This object exhibited a sudden burst of carbon-dioxide sublimation!"). We also added an immersive audio toggle that plays atmospheric background music (inspired by the Zelda Astral Observatory) to elevate the user experience from a dry database into an engaging, emotional journey through space.

Factors the team considered Our primary considerations revolved around performance, accessibility, and open-source licensing compliance:

  • Handling Massive Data: We knew rendering 102 infrared bands over multiple epochs would crash standard browsers. We solved this by splitting the pipeline: using NASA's officially calibrated HiPS maps for smooth visual panning, while reserving Zarr chunk extraction strictly for on-demand scientific number-crunching when a user clicks a target.
  • Scalability: Knowing that SPHEREx data is constantly updating, we designed the backend script to easily query IRSA via SIA2 protocols to pull the latest Quick Release (QR) data seamlessly.
  • Clean-Room UI Implementation: While heavily inspired by the highly effective UX of Stellarium Web (like the bottom toolbar, FoV indicator, and metadata popups), we explicitly engineered 100% original code from scratch to avoid GPL license contamination, ensuring our project strictly adhered to the MIT License required for maximum flexibility.
"We spend our lives trying to decode the whispers of the universe, turning raw numbers and light curves into stories of where we came from." — An inspiring framing often adapted for modern multi-epoch survey pipelines like SPHEREx. -Kanhi Chamoli
